passage: I'm Pooja, and I sit behind Irfan in assembly. Irfan doesn't say the prayer and doesn't make trouble, just stands with hands folded. At lunch, only to me, Irfan said, "There's no god for me, and it feels lonely. Everyone just assumes." I said nothing clever. I moved my tiffin closer. Later in the library Irfan showed me a book on stars and said, "When I read this I feel small in a good way." I also saw Irfan help the caretaker carry chairs without being asked. I can't say the loneliness is gone, but Irfan asked if I'd come to the astronomy club on Friday.

qa.q: What did Irfan show Pooja in the library?
qa.a: Irfan showed Pooja a book on stars.

qa.q: What does Irfan feel about not believing, and how does Pooja know?
qa.a: Irfan feels lonely, because Irfan said so at lunch, and also a sense of awe when reading about the stars.

qa.q: What could Irfan do to feel less alone?
qa.a: Find people, books and values to rely on, such as the astronomy club, and keep the kindness that already shows in helping.

qa.q: How might Pooja's moving the tiffin closer matter to Irfan?
qa.a: It may have shown company without judgement, though Pooja cannot be sure how it felt to Irfan.

grounding: Irfan feels lonely in not believing in any god, and an observer sees awe, ethics and a first move toward people who share Irfan's interests.

passage:
School librarian's note, Class 11, reading records

Kalyani has borrowed nearly every astronomy book we own this term, and now she is starting on philosophy. On Tuesday she stayed after the last bell and asked, almost in a whisper, if there were books "for people who don't believe in God."

She said her whole family prays together every evening and she sits there feeling nothing. "Everyone has something to hold on to. I feel like I'm the only one who doesn't." She looked very alone saying it.

I didn't tell her what to believe. I showed her a shelf of essays by scientists and thinkers, some believers, some not, who wrote about wonder at the universe and about living kindly. I also mentioned the astronomy club, where her classmate Usha goes on Thursdays.

Today she came back with one essay marked up in pencil. She said, "I didn't know you could feel this much awe without a god." She is going to the club with Usha on Thursday.

qa.q: Which books had Kalyani borrowed nearly all of this term?
qa.a: Kalyani had borrowed nearly every astronomy book in the library.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when she asked about books for non-believers?
qa.a: Kalyani felt lonely and isolated, as if she were the only one with nothing to hold on to while her family prayed.

qa.q: How did the librarian help Kalyani without telling her what to believe?
qa.a: The librarian showed her essays by believers and non-believers about wonder and kindness, and pointed her to the astronomy club with Usha.

qa.q: What might Usha feel when Kalyani joins the club?
qa.a: Usha may feel glad to have a classmate who shares her interest, and Kalyani may find she is less alone there.

grounding: It shows a teen who feels she does not believe in any god and is lonely, finding books, people and values to rely on, and awe without belief.

passage:
Navratri, night 5

Everyone went to the pandal again. I said I had a headache. Tanuja texted, "garba??" and I said no. I'm not unwell. I just don't believe any of it, and sitting through the aarti feeling nothing makes me feel like a ghost.

I think I'm the only one in my family who doesn't believe in God. Maybe in the whole colony. That feels so lonely I can't explain it.

So I went up to the terrace. Power cut in half the lane, so the sky was actually dark. I lay on the mat and saw more stars than I ever have in the city. I felt tiny, and it didn't feel bad. It felt huge and quiet. Is that awe? Can I have that without a god?

I wrote down what I actually believe in: honesty, being kind to Dadi, not wasting food, telling the truth even when it's awkward. That's a list. That's something.

Tomorrow I'll tell Tanuja. Maybe she won't laugh.

— Damini

qa.q: Where did Damini go while everyone was at the pandal?
qa.a: Damini went up to the terrace.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling about being the only non-believer?
qa.a: Damini felt deeply lonely, like a ghost sitting through the aarti feeling nothing.

qa.q: What did Damini do that could help in the long run?
qa.a: Damini wrote down a list of personal values and plans to tell Tanuja, which gives Damini something to rely on and a person to share with.

qa.q: How might Tanuja react if Damini tells her?
qa.a: Tanuja might be surprised, but as a friend who invited Damini to garba, she may be curious and kind rather than laughing.

grounding: It shows a teen who does not believe in any god and feels lonely, finding values to rely on and a sense of awe without belief.
